title-group.article-title: Bioinformatic Analysis to Identify Biomarker Candidates of Complex Karyotype Soft Tissue Sarcomas with CDK4-Amplification

abstract.p: Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs), a diverse group of mesenchymal malignancies, are characterized primarily by copy-number alterations rather than a high tumor mutation burden. In this study, we sought to identify expression-based biomarkers in complex karyotype STS (CKS) with CDK4-amplification to support improved therapeutic strategies. Using transcriptome data from National Cancer Center (NCC)-CKS samples, we selected genes whose expression levels were more than two-fold higher or less than half in tumor tissues compared with normal tissues. These genes were further filtered by CDK4-amplification status, resulting in 30 candidates, which were refined to 14 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) based on false discovery rate (FDR) significance. Bioinformatics analyses revealed enriched pathways and gene–gene networks related to redox regulation and growth-factor–driven signal transduction, indicating metabolic alterations that may promote tumor survival in CDK4-amplified CKS. A subset of the 14 genes demonstrated prognostic significance in CDK4-amplified patients from the TCGA cohort. Additionally, immune cell marker analysis showed associations between CDK4-amplification and innate immune cell signatures. Together, our findings identify promising therapeutic and prognostic targets linked to CDK4-amplification in CKS. These biomarkers warrant further investigation and may ultimately contribute to improved clinical outcomes for patients with CKS.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) are mesenchymal malignancies that account for approximately 1% of all cancers (Islami et al., 2021). STSs arise throughout the body, resulting in significant heterogeneity, with up to 100 subtypes identified (Sbaraglia et al., 2021). Ewing sarcoma, synovial sarcoma, and other STS subtypes with distinct genetic features are classified as simple karyotype STSs. Others belong to complex karyotype STSs (CKSs), which are primarily diagnosed based on histological characteristics (Nacev et al., 2020; Sbaraglia et al., 2021). The rarity and heterogeneity of STSs contribute to delayed diagnosis and present challenges in developing precise therapeutic strategies.

Recently, six STS subtypes have been characterized at the molecular level through multiplatform analyses, including whole-exome sequencing, transcriptome profiling, DNA methylation studies, and reverse-phase protein arrays (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017). These studies revealed several key characteristics of STSs, notably that copy number alterations are more prevalent in STSs than in most other cancer types (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017). Further research on undifferentiated sarcomas has reinforced the role of copy number alterations in tumor development, identifying events such as chromothripsis, early haploidy, and whole-genome duplication (Steele et al., 2019).

In adult CKSs, including leiomyosarcomas, myxofibrosarcomas, and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas, copy number–altered subgroups have been proposed as a basis for therapeutic strategies (Kim et al., 2018). These subgroups are categorized into three groups: CDK4 amplification (located on chromosome 12q14–15), RB1 deletion (located on chromosome 13q14), and chromosome-stable tumors. This classification underscores the importance of copy number alterations in understanding STSs (Kim et al., 2018). Notably, PDGFRA has been suggested as a potential therapeutic target in STSs lacking CDK4-amplification (Kim et al., 2018), supporting the development of targeted therapies (Tap et al., 2016). Further validation is required to improve treatment outcomes (Mellgard et al., 2024) by identifying biomarkers for diagnostics, prognostics, and therapeutics in STSs.

CDK4 plays a crucial role in cell cycle progression from the G1 to S phase by phosphorylating RB1 in conjunction with D-type cyclins, thereby releasing E2F1 in response to mitogenic and oncogenic signaling (Suski et al., 2021). Recent single-cell studies have extended the role of CDK4/6 to cell cycle reversal (Cornwell et al., 2023), highlighting potential benefits of targeting CDK4/6 in cancer treatment. CDK4 alterations are primarily driven by chromosome amplification and are frequently correlated with MDM2, which is located on the same chromosome (12q15) (Jardim et al., 2021), including in STSs ((Lavernia et al., 2024). Other neighboring genes, such as GLI1 (Lavernia et al., 2024) and FRS2, have also been considered for targeted therapy, particularly in relation to fibroblast growth factor signaling perturbations in sarcomas (Formisano et al., 2019).

Preclinical studies have shown promising results in targeting CDK4 using three oral selective inhibitors: palbociclib (PD0332991; Ibrance, Pfizer), ribociclib (LEE011; Novartis), and abemaciclib (LY2835219; Eli Lilly & Company). These inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in treating breast cancer, melanoma, liposarcoma, and non–small cell lung cancer (Morrison et al., 2024; Shanabag et al., 2025; Tripathy et al., 2017; VanArsdale et al., 2015). Because CDK4 inhibitors prevent CDK4 or the cyclin D–CDK4 complex from phosphorylating RB1, tumor RB1 expression has been associated with a favorable response to CDK4 inhibition (VanArsdale et al., 2015). In particular, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the use of CDK4/6 inhibitors in combination with endocrine therapy for hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, based on substantial improvements in progression-free survival of up to several months (Rao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024).

In STSs, dysregulation of the CDKN2A–CDK4/6–RB1 pathway has been extensively addressed (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Hsu et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2018). Clinical trials investigating palbociclib and abemaciclib have included patients with sarcoma, such as trial NCT01209598, which focused on liposarcomas (Dickson et al., 2013). Patients with CDK4-amplified, RB1-expressing well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas exhibited significantly improved progression-free survival when treated with palbociclib (Dickson et al., 2016). However, for other STS subtypes, clinical outcomes with CDK4/6 inhibitors have been variable (Hsu et al., 2022). Ongoing efforts to enhance therapeutic efficacy include overcoming drug resistance (Rao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024) and identifying biomarkers to predict response or inform additional therapeutic strategies across different STS subtypes.

Currently, there are limited databases containing both tumor and matched normal tissue samples for validation. However, the National Cancer Center (NCC)-CKS cohort includes matched normal tissues in up to 50% of cases.

In this study, we aimed to identify biomarkers for CKSs with CDK4-amplification, to assess their prognostic value and therapeutic potential. Biomarkers were selected based on mRNA expression levels, which were compared between normal tissues and tumor tissues lacking CDK4-amplification. This approach may help determine the feasibility of these biomarkers for further clinical application.

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: This study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the National Cancer Center, Korea (IRB No.: NCC2017–0062). Written informed consent was obtained from all patients before tissue acquisition, and all samples were stored according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Bioinformatical analyses-differentially expressed gene (DEG) selection
sec.p: We profiled the NCC-CKS transcriptome (Kim et al., 2018) to identify DEGs (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018). Genes with Fragment Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads (FPKM) values less than 10 in all samples were excluded from further analysis. DEGs were filtered based on fold change with p-value thresholds. Hierarchical clustering was performed to generate a heatmap using the iDEP platform (Ge et al., 2018). Genes were selected based on a fold change greater than 2 or less than 0.5, with a p-value of less than 0.05. These results were visualized using volcano plots created in PRISM 9.0 (GraphPad Software, Boston, MA, USA) to illustrate the relationship between gene expression changes and statistical significance. A total of thirty genes were selected from the DEGs analysis. To refine the 30 DEGs, the false discovery rate (FDR) was assessed using two approaches: the Limma method (Ritchie et al., 2015) and the Benjamini–Hochberg (B–H) procedure (Glueck et al., 2008). Specifically, a moderated linear model in limma with B–H FDR correction and a gene-wise t-test applying the same B–H adjustment were used during the selection process. Fourteen genes met the FDR significance threshold (p<0.05) in both analyses, resulting in a final set of 14 DEGs. To compare gene expression levels, the transcriptome of the KNCC-STS1 cell line was utilized (Lee et al., 2023).

sec.title: Bioinformatical analyses-Gene-gene correlation and network analysis
sec.p: To investigate gene-gene correlations, we performed correlation analysis in R using the Cor.mtest, corrplot, and Hmisc packages, based on the Pearson correlation coefficient with associated p-values. Pairwise correlations among the 14 DEGs were analyzed separately for the CDK4-amplified and non-amplified groups using R with the stats, corrplot, and tidyverse packages. For each group, Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated from log-scaled expression values, and corresponding two-sided p-values were obtained using standard correlation tests. CDK4-amplification–specific effects were evaluated by generating a delta-correlation (Δ-correlation) matrix, defined as the difference between the correlation matrices of the amplified and non-amplified groups. The significance of these Δ values was further assessed through a permutation procedure (5,000 iterations), yielding permutation-based p-values for all gene pairs.
Gene-pathway network analysis was performed using the GO biological process database in Cytoscape with the ClueGO and CluePedia plugins (Bindea et al., 2009, 2013).

To assess the correlation between the 14 DEGs and immune cells within tumor microenvironment (TME), we performed a correlation analysis using both the DEGs and 120 previously utilized immune cell–related genes (Becht et al., 2016; Petitprez et al., 2020) in the NCC-CKS cohort as well as the TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohort. Pearson correlation matrices were computed using transposed expression data to evaluate gene–gene co-expression patterns. Heatmaps of the correlation matrices were generated using the pheatmap package from R, with hierarchical clustering applied to visualize the gene co-expression structure.

sec.title: Bioinformatical analyses-Analysis of the DEGs in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas Cohort
sec.p: The 14 DEGs were further analyzed using data from the TCGA PanCancer Atlas (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Liu et al., 2018). Specifically, we obtained transcriptomic data for LGG, GBM, LUAD, and SARC from the TCGA PanCancer Atlas study to validate the expression of the 14 DEGs, using cBioPortal (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Liu et al., 2018) for further validations of 14 DEGs by utilizing cBioportal (Gao et al., 2013). To explore gene distribution in cancers with and without CDK4-amplification, two-dimensional PCA (2D-PCA) was performed using R packages ggplot2 and datasets. Additionally, three-dimensional PCA (3D-PCA) was conducted using R packages including plotly, dplyr, tidytext, pheatmap, and ggplot2.

Gene expression profiles for the fourteen DEGs were analyzed in R using log2-transformed, z-score–normalized values. LUAD samples were excluded, leaving only GBM, LGG, and SARC samples for analysis. CDK4-amplified and non-amplified samples were clustered separately and then merged to generate an ordered heatmap visualization using the ComplexHeatmap package.

sec.title: Statistical analysis of overall survival and Hazard Ratios
sec.p: Copy number, RNA expression, and survival data were obtained from the TCGA PanCancer Atlas database (Liu et al., 2018). Kaplan–Meier survival analysis was conducted to evaluate overall survival based on the mean expression levels of target genes and CDK4-amplification status. Survival curves and statistical comparisons were generated using the R packages survival, survminer, ggplot2, and dplyr. Correlation coefficients and p-values were calculated using the rcorr() function. For gene-level survival assessment within the CDK4-amplified subset, optimal expression thresholds were identified for each gene using maximally selected rank statistics. Based on the optimal threshold, patients were classified into high- and low-expression groups, and Kaplan–Meier curves were generated for each gene. Corresponding univariate Cox proportional hazards models were fitted to estimate hazard ratios (HRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and p-values. Forest plots summarizing gene-specific Cox results were produced using ggplot2.

sec.title: CDK4-Amplification–Associated Gene Expression Analysis
sec.p: To characterize gene expression changes associated with CDK4-amplification, we applied two modeling strategies: a mixed-effects model with cancer type included as a random factor, and an unadjusted linear model. Effect sizes and p-values were obtained from both models, and multiple testing was controlled using the B-H FDR procedure. Expression patterns were further explored using z-score–based heatmap visualization generated with ComplexHeatmap, with samples clustered within amplification groups to preserve group structure. Gene-level distributions were summarized using boxplots. A 14-gene signature score was calculated as the mean z-score across the selected genes, and its ability to distinguish CDK4-amplified tumors was assessed using ROC analysis implemented in pROC. Agreement between the two models was evaluated by comparing their effect-size estimates.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: All data are expressed as percentages of the control and shown as means ± SE. Statistical comparisons between groups were made using Student’s t tests. Values of p<0.05 were considered significant. To analyze multiple testing, p-values were corrected using the B-H FDR procedure.

sec.title: Identification of DEGs associated with CDK4-amplification in the NCC-CKS
sec.p: The NCC-CKS database comprised 14 tumor tissues representing three histological CKS subtypes—leiomyosarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, and undifferentiated sarcoma (including undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, undifferentiated round cell sarcoma, and undifferentiated small cell sarcoma)—along with seven matched normal tissues (Kim et al., 2018). Most tumor tissues (11 of 14) were obtained from patients without preoperative therapy. Thus, transcriptome profiling was considered a reliable approach for understanding tumor characteristics based on gene expression (Fig. 1A). Multiplex genomic DNA polymerase chain reaction using specific primer sets targeting CDK4 and GAPDH supported CDK4-amplification, and CDK4 expression at both the RNA and protein levels was correlated with the transcriptome of the NCC-CKS cohort (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1). Together, these findings demonstrate the reliability of the dataset (Kim et al., 2018) for further analysis.

From the NCC-CKS transcriptome, 4,318 genes with RNA expression levels greater than 10 FPKM were selected for differential expression analysis. Among these, DEGs were identified based on expression levels that were either more than doubled or reduced to less than half in tumor tissues compared with normal tissues, yielding a total of 2,454 genes (Fig. 1B). To identify biomarkers associated with CDK4-amplification, these genes were further filtered according to the CDK4-amplification status in patients (Fig. 1C, 1D), resulting in 30 DEGs. We next assessed false discovery rate significance using the Limma method (Ritchie et al., 2015) and the B–H method (Glueck et al., 2008), which reduced the set to 14 DEGs. Among these, 11 genes were upregulated (SPARC, SEPTIN11, PDGFRB, IFI27, GBP3, CYBRD1, CTDSP2, COL5A2, COL1A1, CCN1, and C1S), while 3 genes were downregulated (NDUFA7, HSPB1, and COX5A). Pearson’s correlation analysis, performed using an R package, revealed several notable relationships among the 14 DEGs (Fig. 1E). Several gene pairs exhibited significantly increased co-expression in CDK4-amplified tumors. Delta-correlation analysis with permutation testing identified marked amplification-specific gains in pairs such as COX5A–PDGFRB and PDGFRB–SPARC (p<0.05), whereas pairs including C1S–GBP3, CCN1–GBP3, and IFI27–COL1A1 showed reduced co-expression under CDK4-amplification. These changes highlight collagen- and receptor-related co-expression patterns characteristic of CDK4-amplified tumors.

sec.title: Enriched pathways associated with 14 DEGs in CKSs with CDK4-amplification
sec.p: To investigate functional gene–pathway associations, we utilized Cytoscape in combination with the ClueGO (Bindea et al., 2009) and CluePedia (Bindea et al., 2013) plugins (Fig. 2). The 14 DEGs mapped to 5 GO pathway categories: vascular endothelial growth factor signaling (HSPB1, PDGFRB), regulation of endothelial cell migration (HSPB1, SPARC), collagen fibril organization (COL1A1, COL5A2), response to hyperoxia (CCN1, COL1A1, PDGFRB), and oxidoreduction-driven active transmembrane transporter activity (COX5A, CYBRD1, NDUFA7) (Fig. 2A). These pathways formed 2 major clusters (Fig. 2B).

Cluster 1, composed predominantly of upregulated genes (SPARC, PDGFRB, CCN1, COL1A1, COL5A2) along with 1 downregulated gene (HSPB1), was enriched for collagen fibril organization, vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, response to hyperoxia, and endothelial cell migration. Cluster 2 consisted of 2 downregulated genes (NDUFA7, COX5A) and 1 upregulated gene (CYBRD1), and was associated with oxidative phosphorylation and electron transport activities, suggesting mitochondrial and metabolic alterations in CDK4-amplified NCC-CKS.

The remaining genes mapped to distinct biological processes, including intrinsic apoptotic signaling (IFI27), complement activation (C1S), and G1/S cell cycle transition (CTDSP2). Although these genes did not cluster independently, IFI27 and C1S participated in pathways involving Cluster 1 genes, indicating functional connectivity. Overall, the 14 DEGs converge on biologically connected pathways relevant to CDK4-amplified NCC-CKS.

sec.title: TCGA-based prognostic insights from DEGs in CDK4-amplified cancers
sec.p: The DEGs identified from the NCC-CKS transcriptome analyses were further validated to assess whether they are representative of tumors with CDK4-amplification across multiple cancer types, using a database comprising 30 cancer studies (Liu et al., 2018) accessed through the iDEP platform across cancer types (Ge et al., 2018). In addition, their potential association with CDK4-amplification and patient prognosis was evaluated using corresponding clinical information from the same database (Liu et al., 2018). The TCGA PanCancer Atlas study includes 30 cancer types, among which, four—low-grade glioma (LGG), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), glioblastoma (GBM), and sarcoma (SARC; STSs)—were selected based on copy number alteration frequency (4%-18%) and the number of cases with CDK4-amplification (at least 20 cases). The 14 DEGs were used for hierarchical clustering and principal component analysis (PCA) (Greenacre et al., 2022). PCA was performed using the R packages RColorBrewer and pheatmap for clustering, and datasets and ggplot2 for visualization. SARC (44 of 251 cases CDK4-amplified), LGG (21 of 511), and GBM (27 of 148) exhibited distinct tumor distributions according to CDK4-amplification status (Fig. 3). By contrast, LUAD (28 of 507) did not show clear separation. Accordingly, SARC, LGG, and GBM were selected for further analysis to explore prognostic implications. In three-dimensional PCA, each of the functional gene sets contributed uniquely, underscoring the relevance of the DEGs to CDK4-amplification.

Next, the association between CDK4-amplification, DEG expression, and prognosis was examined (Fig. 4). Within the TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohort, the three tumor types—SARC, LGG, and GBM—were stratified according to CDK4-amplification status (amplified vs. non-amplified). The prognostic impact of each DEG on overall survival was evaluated using a Cox proportional hazards model (Fig. 4A). High- and low-signature groups were defined using an optimal cutpoint determined by surv_cutpoint, and this classification was applied consistently across both Kaplan–Meier survival analyses and Cox proportional hazards modeling in CDK4-amplified tumors (Fig. 4).

In the univariate Cox analysis, 11 genes were significantly associated with prognosis in tumors with CDK4 amplification: 5 genes (SPARC, HSPB1, PDGFRB, COL1A1, and COL5A2) from Cluster 1, 2 genes (CYBRD1 and NDUFA7) from Cluster 2, and 4 genes (IFI27, CTDSP2, GBP3, and C1S) from the unclustered group (Fig. 4A). A similar pattern was observed in both the Cox model and Kaplan–Meier analyses (Fig. 4B). Together, these results support a strong association between the expression of 11 DEGs and increased survival risk in CDK4-amplified tumors.

sec.title: Tumor microenvironmental insights from DEGs in CDK4-amplified cancers
sec.p: Next, we investigated whether DEGs associated with CDK4-amplification have functional relevance in the TME, which may be critical for informing anticancer therapeutic strategies. To address this, we analyzed three cancer types stratified by CDK4-amplification status, using a panel of 120 immune phenotype–related genes (Becht et al., 2016; Petitprez et al., 2020). Gene–gene correlation analysis in CDK4-amplified tumors revealed several distinct clusters involving the 14 DEGs and immune phenotype–related genes (Fig. 5A). Among these, two DEGs—NDUFA7 and COX5A—formed an independent cluster, indicating limited interaction with immune-related genes. By contrast, three DEGs—C1S, IFI27, and GBP3—clustered with immune phenotype–related genes involved in both innate and adaptive immune responses, suggesting a potential role in modulating TME immunity (Fig. 5A, 5B).

Additionally, two mixed clusters were identified: one containing CTDSP2, SEPTIN11, and HSPB1, and another comprising CYBRD1, SPARC, COL1A1, COL5A2, and PDGFRB. Both clusters showed diffuse, low-strength associations with a broad range of immune cell–related genes, along with notable links to non-immune endothelial cell signatures. The cluster containing CYBRD1, SPARC, COL1A1, COL5A2, and PDGFRB was predominantly linked to endothelial cell–related genes (Fig. 5). This observation prompted us to examine further whether innate immune cell markers exhibit CDK4-amplification–dependent expression patterns in the NCC-CKS cohort and TCGA tumors.

As expected, markers for monocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils were more highly expressed in NCC-CKS tumors with than without CDK4-amplification (Fig. 6A). Expression levels of markers for macrophages and monocytes, together with five DEGs including IFI27, C1S, and HSPB1, were compared between tumors with and without CDK4-amplification in both the NCC-CKS cohort (Fig. 6B) and the three TCGA cancer types (Fig. 6C). Most markers and DEGs showed significant alterations depending on CDK4-amplification status, supporting a role for CDK4-associated DEGs in TME immune function.

Among markers for monocytes and macrophages, RASSF4, a monocyte marker, was upregulated, whereas MRC1, a marker for M2 macrophages, was downregulated in the NCC-CKS cohort. Interestingly, these markers exhibited opposite expression patterns within individual subsets depending on CDK4-amplification status. Notably, only three cancer types showed statistically significant alterations. Among the DEGs, IFI27 and C1S were upregulated in both the NCC-CKS cohort and across the three cancer types analyzed. By contrast, HSPB1 was consistently downregulated in both NCC-CKS and the TCGA cancer datasets, suggesting a distinct expression pattern of CDK4-amplification–associated DEGs. Together, these findings underscore the importance of considering the role of innate immune cells within the TME when evaluating prognosis and developing therapeutic strategies for tumors harboring CDK4-amplification, including CKS.

sec.title: Possible therapeutic suggestions from DEGs in CDK4-amplified cancers
sec.p: Furthermore, we investigated whether DEGs associated with CDK4-amplification could represent actionable targets with potential therapeutic relevance. First, we screened drugs linked to the DEGs (Supplementary Table 2). Notably, HSPB1, PDGFRB, and C1S showed extensive gene–drug interactions, each associated with more than 10 compounds, irrespective of FDA approval status. Based on gene–drug network analysis, all 14 DEGs were identified as directly targetable, with the majority of corresponding drugs functioning as inhibitors. However, DEG expression levels and functional activity should be considered independently prior to clinical application (Fig. 4B). Although further experimental validation is required to support combining DEG-targeted agents with CDK4/6 inhibitors, these findings suggest that targeting DEGs linked to TME-associated biology may offer an indirect yet promising strategy to enhance therapeutic responses.

In the NCC-CKS cohort, three DEGs associated with TME immune cells displayed CDK4 amplification–specific expression patterns (Fig. 7A). Among these, IFI27 was significantly upregulated in CDK4-amplified tumors, whereas HSPB1 showed markedly reduced expression. Interestingly, the KNCC-STS1 cell line—recently established from undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma tissue (Lee et al., 2023) and known to harbor CDK4-amplification—exhibited a similar RNA-level expression pattern. This suggests that IFI27 and HSPB1 expression patterns in CDK4-amplified tumors may reflect intrinsic transcriptional features of the cancer cells themselves. By contrast, C1S was significantly associated with CDK4-amplification in tumor tissues but not in the KNCC-STS1 cell line, implying that its expression is likely derived from non-malignant components of the TME. Based on these observations, we focused subsequent analyses on IFI27 and HSPB1, evaluating their potential roles in modulating immune functions within the TME and influencing tumor progression (Fig. 7B), as well as their involvement in gene–drug interaction networks (Fig. 7C).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: The expression of cell cycle–related genes in sarcomas has been widely studied and is recognized as clinically relevant (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Dickson et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2018; Suski et al., 2021). However, therapeutic responses to CDK4/6 inhibitors in CKSs—including undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and myxofibrosarcoma—remain unpredictable, underscoring the need for further investigation. While these inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in certain cases of liposarcoma, their effectiveness in the relatively rare CKS subtypes is still unclear. This uncertainty is largely attributable to the limited availability of appropriate research models, which poses a substantial challenge for conducting the basic and translational studies needed to improve treatment responsiveness.

In this study, we identified 14 DEGs that are significantly altered in tumors, compared to matched normal tissues, and are associated with CDK4-amplification in the NCC-CKS cohort (Fig. 1). To assess the therapeutic relevance of these DEGs, we conducted a comprehensive analysis across four key dimensions (Fig. 8).

Pathway enrichment analysis grouped the DEGs into three categories—Cluster 1, Cluster 2, and unclustered genes—each characterized by distinct biological features (Fig. 2). These clusters also showed consistent associations with CDK4-amplification in additional cancer types from the TCGA PanCancer Atlas, specifically in the LGG, GBM, and SARC cohorts, each of which included more than ten tumors with CDK4-amplification (Fig. 3). By integrating data from these three TCGA cohorts, we evaluated further the prognostic relevance of the DEGs (Fig. 4) and identified 11 genes that were significantly associated with overall survival in tumors harboring CDK4-amplification. Further analysis of DEG interactions with immune cell–related genes revealed a close relationship between three DEGs and components of the innate immune system (Fig. 5). These genes were also associated with altered expression of immune-related markers in both the NCC-CKS cohort and the combined TCGA cohorts, depending on CDK4-amplification status (Fig. 6). Taken together, the observed links between DEGs, the TME, and clinical outcomes suggest that indirect therapeutic strategies—particularly those aimed at modulating the TME through regulation of innate immune pathways—may represent a promising avenue for improving treatment responses in CDK4-amplified CKSs (Fig. 7).

The 14 DEGs were specifically associated with CKS tumors harboring CDK4 amplification (11 upregulated and 3 downregulated). These genes were primarily linked to oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis (Fig. 2). Metabolic reprogramming toward a more glycolytic state may be explained by CDK4-amplification in CKSs, which correlates with increased mitochondrial size and function in cyclin D1–deficient mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Wang et al., 2006). Cyclin D1 expression has been shown to activate aldolase, facilitating the glycolytic pathway, as well as carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 2, aspartate transcarbamylase, and dihydroorotase (CAD) for pyrimidine synthesis through phosphorylation by CDK4 in hepatocytes (Wu et al., 2023), supporting a role for CDK4 in metabolic reprogramming. Additionally, this reprogramming has been linked to the mTOR pathway in pancreatic cancers in response to CDK4/6 inhibition (Franco et al., 2016). In metastatic breast cancers, CDK4/6 inhibitors have been associated with metabolic alterations that render the TME more vulnerable to T cell–based therapy (Rao et al., 2023). We are prospectively expanding our CKS cohort to validate further this metabolic reprogramming and its potential implications for therapeutic strategy development.

Type I interferon signaling has been implicated in a range of immune responses, including resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors, particularly in breast cancer (De Angelis et al., 2021), as well as responses to immune checkpoint blockade in melanoma (Holzgruber et al., 2024). In metastatic breast cancers, interferon-regulated genes, including IFI27—an interferon-α–inducible protein—are expressed at lower levels compared with primary breast cancers, resulting in impaired immune function within the TME (Shojaei and McLean, 2025). These findings support a role for IFI27 and related genes in regulating immune activity in the TME. Accordingly, indirect targeting of IFI27 expression through its splicing regulator NSRP1 (Yu et al., 2025) or the ubiquitin ligase PJA2 (Schiefer and Hale, 2024) may represent a potential therapeutic approach.

HSPB1, a redox-sensitive small heat shock protein, functions as a molecular chaperone and plays a crucial role in mitochondrial metabolic processes (Adriaenssens et al., 2023), as well as in the regulation of cell death (Sun et al., 2015). Recent studies have identified HSPB1 as a key factor influencing cellular responses to abemaciclib (a CDK4/6 inhibitor), venetoclax (a BCL-2 inhibitor), or their combination (Sun et al., 2015). In addition to its intracellular roles, HSPB1 has been implicated in modulation of the TME by influencing cytokine secretion from monocytic cells (Ogbodo et al., 2023). In an in vivo sepsis model, HSPB1 was shown to protect mice by modulating immune responses (Breed et al., 2018). Given these diverse functions, targeting HSPB1 in CKSs with CDK4-amplification may offer therapeutic benefit through both direct effects on tumor cells and indirect modulation of the immune microenvironment. However, further studies are needed to validate HSPB1 as a therapeutic target in this context.

Finally, we identified and categorized 14 DEGs through a stepwise selection process comparing normal tissues, tumors, and tumors stratified by CDK4-amplification status. Using comprehensive bioinformatic analyses, we assessed the association of these DEGs with key biological features, including pathway involvement, prognostic relevance, TME immune cell correlations, and drug availability. Although further validation is required to confirm clinical applicability, these 14 DEGs demonstrated consistent biological relevance and exhibited distinct associations with CDK4-amplified tumors beyond CKSs. These findings support the potential extension of therapeutic strategies to CKSs through repurposing FDA-approved drugs or treatment modalities currently used in other CDK4-amplified malignancies, such as LGG and GBM. Moreover, the 14-gene signature may represent a biologically meaningful and prognostic marker of CDK4-amplification, highlighting its potential relevance for both tumor biology and clinical stratification.

caption.p: Identification of DEGs associated with CDK4-amplification in the NCC-CKS. (A) Overview of Research Design. This image was created with BioRender (https://biorender.com/) and modified. (B) Heatmap for DEGs between tumors and normal (tumor(T)/normal(N)>2 or T/N<0.5, p<0.05). (C, D) Volcano plots to show DEGs between tumors with CDK4-amplification and matched normal (C) and between tumors with CDK4-amplification and non-amplified (D). Blue dots represent downregulated genes, red dots represent upregulated genes, and gray dots represent unchanged genes in tumors with CDK4-amplification. (E) Pairwise correlations among the 14 DEGs were analyzed separately for the CDK4-amplified (Left top panel) and non-amplified groups (Left bottom panel). CDK4-amplification–specific effects were evaluated by generating a delta-correlation (Δ-correlation) matrix, defined as the difference between the correlation matrices of the amplified and non-amplified groups (Right panel). The significance of these Δ values was further assessed through a permutation procedure (5,000 iterations), yielding permutation-based p-values for all gene pairs. The correlation matrix between genes was visualized using R packages, with significance levels indicated (*p<0.05). Positive correlations are represented in red, while negative correlations are shown in blue. The size of the circles corresponds to the correlation coefficient, and the color intensity reflects the strength and direction of the correlation. DEG: Differentially expressed gene, NCC-CKS: National Cancer Center-complex karyotype soft tissue sarcoma, FDR: false discovery rate.

Functional gene-pathway network of DEGs associated with CDK4-amplification in NCC-CKS. (A) Gene-gene and gene-pathway network analysis using Cytoscape with the ClueGO and CluePedia plugins. Functionally grouped networks are represented as nodes linked based on their kappa score level, with only the most significant term per group labeled. Node size indicates the significance of term enrichment. The distribution of two clusters (Cluster 1 and Cluster 2) is visualized within the network. Genes are represented as dots, with upregulated and downregulated genes displayed in red and blue text, respectively. Colored lines indicate gene-pathway interactions. (B) Biological pathway enrichment analysis of the 30 DEGs using GO pathways in R with the clusterProfiler package. The intensity and size of the circles correspond to the p-adjusted value and gene counts, respectively. The Gene Ratio represents the proportion of genes of interest within this dataset compared to the total number of genes. DEG: Differentially expressed gene, NCC-CKS: National Cancer Center-complex karyotype soft tissue sarcoma, GO: Gene ontology.

The 14 DEGs in CDK4-amplified cancers across three TCGA studies. (A) Heatmaps illustrate the expression patterns of 14 DEGs with available data, comparing tumors with and without CDK4-amplification across three cancer types. Tumors with CDK4-amplification are marked by an orange bar, and non-amplified tumors by a gray bar. Cancer types are color-coded: orange for GBM (glioblastoma), pink for LGG (low-grade glioma), and green for SARC (sarcoma). (B) The number of samples with CDK4-amplification in each cancer cohort was expression, respectively. (C) PCA results of functional gene clusters in each cancer study, stratified by CDK4-amplification status. Red dots represent patients with CDK4-amplification, and gray dots represent patients without CDK4-amplification. Three-dimensional PCA of 14 DEGs in the three cancer studies, showing separation based on CDK4-amplification status (Left top). DEG: Differentially expressed gene, NCC-CKS: National Cancer Center-complex karyotype soft tissue sarcoma, PCA: Principal component analysis.

Association of DEGs with prognosis in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas in relation to CDK4-amplification. (A) Forest plots showing hazard ratios for overall survival based on the expression levels of 14 DEGs in patients with CDK4-amplification. Statistical significance: *p<0.05, **p<0.01, and ***p<0.001. CI indicates confidence interval. (B) Overall survival of SARC, LGG, and GBM patients with CDK4-amplification, stratified by high or low expression of each gene. Red lines represent patients with high gene expression, and blue lines represent those with low expression. p-values are shown in the plot boxes. DEG: Differentially expressed gene, LGG: Low-grade glioma, GBM: Glioblastoma, SARC: Sarcoma.

Association of DEGs with the Tumor Microenvironment (TME) in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas in Relation to CDK4-amplification. (A) Correlation heatmap showing 14 DEGs and 120 immune phenotype-related genes in three tumor types—SARC, LGG, and GBM—with CDK4-amplification, based on data from the TCGA PanCancer Atlas. Specific clusters are highlighted with boxes containing gene lists. The red and pink boxes indicate clusters demonstrating meaningful correlation between DEGs and immune cell-related genes. Green arrows point to DEGs within the correlation clusters. (B) Gene list of the largest cluster identified in panel (A). Genes are categorized by immune cell type, function, and involvement in immune systems. Genes highlighted in green are associated with the innate immune system, while those in blue are associated with the adaptive immune system. DEG: Differentially expressed gene, LGG: Low-grade glioma, GBM: Glioblastoma, SARC: Sarcoma.

Expression of Innate Immune Cell Markers in the NCC-CKS Cohort and Three TCGA Cancer Types. (A) Heatmap showing the expression of selected innate immune cell markers in the NCC-CKS tumors. The orange bar at the top of the heatmap denotes tumors with CDK4-amplification, while the gray bar indicates tumors without CDK4-amplification. Immune gene markers are color-coded by cell type: sky blue for monocytes, deep blue for macrophages, light pink for immunosuppressive markers, and violet for neutrophils. (B, C) Expression levels of immune cell-type markers (left panel) and five DEGs (right panel) in tumors with or without CDK4-amplification in the NCC-CKS cohort (B) and the three TCGA cancer types (C), respectively. Immune gene markers are color coded by cell type: sky blue for monocytes, blue for M1 macrophages and deep blue for M2 macrophages. Gene expression is represented as log2 (FPKM+1). Mean values are indicated by gray bars. Statistical significance: *p<0.05, **p<0.01, and ***p<0.001. NCC-CKS: National Cancer Center-complex karyotype soft tissue sarcoma, FPKM: Fragment Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads.

Targeting the TME in CDK4-amplified Tumors via IFI27, HSPB1, and C1S. (A) Expression levels of IFI27, HSPB1, and C1S in the NCC-CKS cohort and KNCC-STS1 cell line, derived from an undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma with CDK4-amplification. Sample groups include: Normal tissue (N), Tumor tissue (T), tumors without CDK4-amplification (T/NO), tumors with CDK4-amplification (T/Only), and the KNCC-STS1 cell line (STS1) harboring CDK4-amplification (STS1/Yes). *Note: RNA-seq expression analysis of the STS1 cell line was based on a single, non-replicated sample, unlike the other samples. Statistical significance is indicated as follows: *p<0.05; **p<0.01; ***p<0.001. (B) Hypothetical roles of IFI27 and HSPB1 in tumor progression: Top right: IFI27 expression may play a role in resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors. Bottom right: HSPB1 may enhance immune activation, potentially suppressing tumor progression. (C) Gene-drug interaction network for IFI27, HSPB1, C1S and associated genes based on the DGIdb database. FDA approved drugs are shown in skyblue. Three DEGs—IFI27, HSPB1, and C1S—are shown in yellow. Gene neighbors with drug interactions are in pink, while those without drug interactions are in grey. Red blocks indicate inhibitory interactions between genes and drugs. NCC-CKS: National Cancer Center-complex karyotype soft tissue sarcoma, FDA: the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Multi-dimensional categorization of 14 DEGs associated with CDK4-amplification in CKSs. (A) Schematic overview of the multi-dimensional analysis conducted on the 14 DEGs. This figure was created with BioRender (https://biorender.com/) and subsequently modified. (B) Summary of associations between the 14 DEGs and key biological features, including pathway involvement, prognostic significance, TME immune cell correlations, and drug availability. Genes are categorized into Cluster 1 (light pink), Cluster 2 (pink), and unclustered (violet). Significant associations with prognosis are highlighted in green, correlations with TME immune cell markers are shown in yellow, and genes with available drugs are indicated in blue. DEG: Differentially expressed gene, CKS: Complex karyotype soft tissue sarcoma, TME: Tumor microenvironment.
